label: PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 · vLLM batch 1 · Batch invariance off

findings.summary: Batch invariance was off. This setup was superseded after same-engine output variation was confirmed. NACA OCR took 10.54 s; the busiest GPU averaged 91.8% busy, compared with 28.8% in the accepted native baseline.
observations: The ordinary NACA call took 12.59 s: OCR 10.54 s (83.7%), embedding 1.91 s (15.2%). It follows one warm-up and excludes the separate instrumented call.
GPU busy means over the OCR window were 36.9%, 54.7%, 91.8%, 0.0% on GPUs 0–3. Shorter pages finish early; GPU 3 has no assigned page.

GPU 2 determines OCR completion. It averaged 70.8 W against its 72 W limit. One-second telemetry provides only 10 OCR-window samples per GPU; GPU busy is sampled activity, not percentage of peak compute.
Scheduler samples every 100 ms observed up to 1 running region(s) on each active recognizer. The complete evaluator sweep also recorded actual response batch sizes in batching-validation.json.

Bounded traces capture 32 engine iterations on each active recognizer. Iterations can include multiple regions, vision, prefill and decoding; kernel counts are not directly comparable with native kernels per decode forward.

All 71 NACA regions ended with EOS. The instrumented output still fails exact OCR matching at 2 LaTeX spacing sites; all chunk embeddings remain above 0.99 cosine. English and Spanish evaluator calls also fail some embedding comparisons.
Hardware counters for achieved compute throughput, DRAM bandwidth and occupancy were not collected. Physical VRAM and server scheduler activity are separate from GPU compute utilization.
findings.next_step: Use vLLM batch 1 with batch invariance enabled as the baseline; compare batch 4 page routing and batch 4 across all GPUs against it.
findings.optimization: Distribute detected recognition regions across all four GPUs to reduce page imbalance, then check output matching against the vLLM baseline.
